lessons.title: Watering schedules for dry and rainy seasons
lessons.body: Watering is the difference between a struggling seedling and a strong fruit tree. In the dry season, young trees need 10 to 20 liters of water every 2 to 3 days. For a 1-year-old tree, give 10 liters; for a 2-year-old, 20 liters. Pour slowly around the base, not on the leaves. Early morning or late evening is best to reduce evaporation. In very hot areas, water every day if the soil is sandy. A simple test: dig 10 cm down; if the soil is dry, water. In the rainy season, stop watering if you get rain every week. But if rains are light, still check the soil. Too much water can rot roots, so make sure water drains away. Dig a small basin around each tree to hold water. Mulch heavily to keep moisture in. If you have a borehole or well, use a bucket and a cup to measure. For 10 trees, you need 100 to 200 liters per watering. Collect rainwater from roofs into drums. A 200-liter drum can water 10 young trees for one dry week. In drought, reduce watering to once a week but give more waterâ30 liters per treeâso it goes deep. Never water at midday; you lose half to evaporation. Keep a simple calendar: mark watering days. If leaves wilt in the afternoon, that's normal; if they wilt in the morning, water immediately. For mature trees, water deeply once a week in dry season. In rainy season, ensure no standing water around trunks. Make small channels to drain excess. Remember: young trees die more from lack of water than from pests. So priority number one is a steady water supply.

lessons.title: Weeding and mulching to conserve water and suppress weeds
lessons.body: Weeds steal water and food from your young trees. A weed-free orchard gives you bigger harvests. Start weeding when weeds are smallâbefore they seed. Use a hand hoe or machete. For a small orchard of 20 trees, you can weed in one morning. Weed in a 1-meter circle around each tree. Don't dig deep near the trunk; you can cut roots. Pull weeds by hand near the base. After weeding, apply mulch. Mulch is any dry plant material: grass, straw, maize stalks, banana leaves, or dry leaves. Spread a layer 5 to 10 cm thick around the tree, but keep it 10 cm away from the trunk to prevent rot. Mulch does three things: stops weeds, keeps soil moist, and cools the soil. In dry season, mulch can reduce watering by half. You can also use living mulch like beans or groundnuts between treesâthey cover the soil and you get a crop. But don't let them climb the trees. For weed control without chemicals, use a sharp hoe weekly during rainy season. If you have serious weeds like couch grass, dig out the roots. Mulch materials: collect from around your farm. One tree needs about 2 buckets of mulch. Reapply every 3 months. In rainy season, weeds grow fastâweed every 2 weeks. In dry season, weed once a month. A thick mulch of dry grass also stops soil erosion. If you have no mulch, use stones or old cardboard. But organic mulch adds nutrients as it rots. Never burn weeds; use them as mulch after drying. Keep a weed-free strip along the tree row. This simple habit doubles growth in the first two years.

lessons.title: Pruning and training young trees for easy harvest
lessons.body: Pruning shapes the tree so you can pick fruit without a ladder. Start when the tree is 1 year old. First, remove all branches growing from the bottom 60 cm of the trunk. These are called water sprouts and they steal energy. Next, choose 3 to 5 main branches that grow outward in different directionsâlike the spokes of a wheel. These will be your scaffold branches. Cut off any branch that crosses or rubs another. Use sharp secateurs or a pruning saw. Make clean cuts at a slight angle, 1 cm above a bud. Don't leave stubs. For young trees, prune in the dry season when the tree is dormant. Remove dead, diseased, or broken branches anytime. Training means tying branches to spread them. Use soft string or banana fiber. Tie a branch to a stake in the ground to pull it outward. This opens the center for sunlight. For easy harvest, keep the tree height under 2.5 meters. Cut the top of the main stem to force side branches. Repeat every year. In the first 3 years, remove all flowers so the tree puts energy into roots and branches. For mature trees, remove old wood to encourage new fruiting wood. A well-pruned tree gives 30% more fruit. Tools: a pruning saw, secateurs, and a ladder for tall branches. Always disinfect tools with spirit or bleach between trees to stop disease. Prune no more than 1/3 of the tree at once. After pruning, burn or remove cuttings to prevent pests. If you see sap oozing, it's normal. Pruning also lets air flow, reducing fungal diseases. Do it every year for strong, easy-to-pick trees.

lessons.title: Applying manure and compost without buying expensive fertilizers
lessons.body: You don't need to buy fertilizer. Manure and compost are free and better for your soil. Start with animal manure: cow, goat, chicken, or rabbit. Fresh manure can burn roots, so let it rot for 2 to 3 months. Pile it up, keep it moist, and turn it every 2 weeks. For compost, layer dry leaves, grass, kitchen scraps, and manure. Make a pile 1 meter high. Turn it every week. In 6 to 8 weeks, it becomes dark, crumbly, and smells like earth. Apply manure or compost in a ring around the tree, 20 cm away from the trunk. For a young tree, use 1 to 2 buckets (10 to 20 liters) per year. For a mature tree, use 4 to 6 buckets. Spread it on top of the soil, then cover with mulch. Don't dig it in deepâearthworms will mix it. Best time to apply: start of rainy season. That way nutrients wash into the soil. You can also make manure tea: put a bucket of manure in a sack, soak in 20 liters of water for 3 days, then use the liquid to water your trees. This is a quick boost. For potted seedlings, mix 1 part compost with 3 parts soil. Never use fresh chicken manure directlyâit's too strong. If you have no animals, use kitchen waste, grass clippings, and ash (small amounts). Ash adds potassium. A good compost pile needs air, water, and green and brown materials. Green: fresh grass, kitchen scraps. Brown: dry leaves, straw. Alternate layers. Keep it as wet as a squeezed sponge. In 2 months, you have free fertilizer. This improves soil, holds water, and gives you healthier trees.

lessons.title: Integrated pest management using local plants and traps
lessons.body: Pests don't have to mean chemicals. Use local plants and simple traps. First, scout your trees weekly. Look under leaves and on new shoots. If you see aphids, whiteflies, or caterpillars, act fast. A strong spray of water can knock off many pests. For aphids, spray a mix of 1 liter water, 1 tablespoon liquid soap, and 1 crushed garlic clove. Spray in the evening. For caterpillars, handpick them and drop in soapy water. Use neem: soak 1 kg of crushed neem leaves in 10 liters of water for 24 hours, then strain and spray. Neem works on many insects. For fruit flies, make traps: cut a plastic bottle, put a little vinegar and sugar inside, and hang it on the tree. The flies go in and drown. For ants, which farm aphids, wrap a band of grease or sticky sap around the trunk. For birds, hang shiny CDs or scarecrows. Plant marigolds and basil between treesâthey repel nematodes and some insects. For rodents, use traps or encourage owls by putting up a perch. For larger animals, a simple fence of thorny branches works. Always remove and destroy infested fruits and leaves. Don't put them in compost. If you must use a chemical, choose one like pyrethrum (from chrysanthemum) and spray only the affected tree. Wear gloves and a mask. Rotate crops and keep the orchard clean. A healthy tree resists pests better, so water and feed well. Check your traps every 3 days. This method saves money and keeps your family safe.

lessons.title: Hands-on: Making a simple drip irrigation system from plastic bottles
lessons.body: You can water your trees slowly with a plastic bottle. This is perfect for dry season. Take a 2-liter plastic bottle. Remove the cap. Poke 3 to 5 small holes in the cap using a hot nail or needle. Fill the bottle with water. Screw the cap back on. Dig a small hole 10 cm deep next to your young tree, about 20 cm from the trunk. Turn the bottle upside down and bury the neck in the soil, so the cap is underground. The water will drip slowly into the root zone. One bottle lasts 2 to 3 days. For a bigger tree, use a 5-liter jerrycan. Poke holes in the lid, fill, and hang it on a stake with the lid down. You can also cut the bottom off a bottle, invert it, and plant it next to the treeâfill it and water goes directly to roots. For a small orchard, set up one bottle per tree. Check the holes if water stops; clean them with a needle. In very hot weather, make more holes. This system saves water because it goes straight to the roots, not to weeds. You can add a little compost tea to the bottle. For 20 trees, you need 20 bottles. Collect them from shops or homes. This costs almost nothing. If you have a tank, run a hose with small holesâbut bottles are easier. Make a frame from sticks to hold the bottle upright. Bury the bottle so it doesn't fall. This is a simple drip system that any farmer can build in one hour. It keeps trees alive during drought and uses 70% less water than pouring from a bucket.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Orchard Management for Small-Scale Farmers

An orchard is a business asset. Every watering can, every mulch layer, every pruned branch is an investment decision that affects yield, fruit quality, and the price you can command at market. This practical reference gives you field-ready methods to keep young fruit trees alive through dry seasons, suppress weeds without costly herbicides, build soil fertility from on-farm materials, and set up a low-cost drip irrigation system from plastic bottles. The goal is simple: lower your cost per kilogram of fruit and raise your margin per tree.

Small-scale orchards in Africa typically face three constraints: unreliable rainfall, expensive inputs, and labour bottlenecks at harvest. The techniques below are designed around those realities. They are low-capital, locally sourced, and proven across smallholder systems in East, West, and Southern Africa. Treat this module as an operating manualâadapt the numbers to your own rainfall, soil type, and market.

1. Watering Schedules for Dry and Rainy Seasons

Young trees are most vulnerable in their first two years. A tree that suffers water stress in year one will never catch up. The rule of thumb: water deeply and less often, so roots grow downward rather than staying near the surface.

Dry season (no effective rain for 2+ weeks): Water young trees (1â2 years) with 10â20 litres per tree every 3â4 days in sandy soil, or every 5â7 days in clay-loam. Mature trees (3+ years) need 40â80 litres every 7â10 days depending on species and canopy size. Water in the early morning or late afternoon to reduce evaporation. Mulch heavily (see next section) to cut frequency by 30â50%.

Rainy season: Do not stop watering entirelyâcheck soil moisture at 15 cm depth. If the soil crumbles rather than forms a ball, irrigate. The main risk in the rainy season is waterlogging, which causes root rot. Ensure drainage channels around tree basins, especially in clay soils. Reduce watering to once every 7â10 days only if rainfall is below 25 mm per week.

Critical stages: Flowering, fruit set, and fruit sizing are the highest water-demand periods. A shortage at fruit set causes drop; a shortage at sizing reduces marketable fruit weight. Plan your irrigation calendar around these stages, not just around calendar months.

2. Weeding and Mulching to Conserve Water and Suppress Weeds

Weeds compete for the same water and nutrients your trees need. In a young orchard, unchecked weeds can reduce growth by 30â50%. Mulching is the cheapest weed suppressor and water conserver available to a smallholder.

Weeding: Keep a 1-metre weed-free ring around each young tree. Hand-hoe shallowly (5â10 cm) to avoid damaging feeder roots. Weed before seed setâevery 3â4 weeks in the rainy season, every 6â8 weeks in the dry season. Slashing between rows is acceptable for mature trees but not for young ones.

Mulching: Apply a 7â10 cm layer of dry grass, maize stover, banana leaves, or coffee husks, leaving a 10 cm gap around the trunk to prevent collar rot. Mulch reduces evaporation by up to 70%, moderates soil temperature, and adds organic matter as it decomposes. Reapply every 3â4 months. In dry areas, mulch can mean the difference between a tree living and dying in its first dry season.

Table 1: Watering and Mulching Frequency by Season and Tree Age

Tree Age Dry Season Watering Rainy Season Watering Mulch Reapplication Weeding Frequency
0â1 year 10 L every 3â4 days (sandy) / 5â7 days (loam) Only if rainfall <25 mm/week Every 3 months Every 3 weeks
1â2 years 15â20 L every 4â5 days Check soil; irrigate if dry at 15 cm Every 3â4 months Every 4 weeks
3+ years 40â80 L every 7â10 days Usually none unless drought Every 4â6 months Every 6â8 weeks

Sources: FAO, Irrigation Water Management: Irrigation Scheduling (FAO Training Manual No. 4, 1989); KALRO, Fruit Tree Production Manual for Smallholder Farmers (2016).

3. Pruning and Training Young Trees for Easy Harvest

Pruning is not cosmeticâit shapes the tree for light penetration, airflow, and reachable fruit. A well-trained tree produces more marketable fruit and costs less to harvest.

Training (years 1â3): Select 3â5 main scaffold branches spaced evenly around the trunk, starting 60â80 cm above ground. Remove competing shoots. This opens the centre so sunlight reaches inner fruit. For mango, avocado, and citrus, aim for an open-centre or modified-leader shape.

Pruning (year 3 onward): Remove dead, diseased, and crossing branches. Thin overcrowded growth to improve airflow and reduce fungal disease. Keep the canopy height within reachâideally below 2.5â3 m for easy harvest without ladders. Prune in the dry season after harvest to reduce disease entry. Always use sharp, clean tools and disinfect between trees.

SAFETY WARNING: Pruning and clearing orchards with machetes or axes causes serious hand and leg injuries every season. Always wear closed shoes, long trousers, and gloves. Never prune above shoulder height while standing on a makeshift platform. Use a pole pruner or a stable ladder. Keep a basic first-aid kit with antiseptic and bandages on site. If you use a chainsaw, wear eye and ear protection and never work alone. In malaria-endemic areas, wear long sleeves and repellent during early morning and evening work.

4. Applying Manure and Compost Without Buying Expensive Fertilizers

You do not need imported fertilizer to grow good fruit. Well-made compost and aged manure supply nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and micronutrients while improving soil structure and water-holding capacity.

Compost making: Build a heap with alternating layers of dry material (maize stalks, dry leaves) and green material (kitchen waste, fresh weeds, grass). Add a handful of wood ash and a little soil. Keep it as moist as a wrung-out cloth. Turn every 2â3 weeks. Ready in 6â10 weeks when it smells earthy and is dark and crumbly.

Manure: Use only well-aged manure (3+ months) to avoid burning roots and spreading pathogens. Apply 1â2 buckets (10â20 kg) per young tree per year, spread in a ring at the drip line, then cover with mulch. Do not pile manure against the trunk.

Application timing: Apply compost or manure at the start of the rainy season and again mid-season. For fruit trees, a split application matches nutrient release to growth flushes and fruit development. This replaces or reduces purchased fertilizer, cutting input costs by 40â70% for smallholders.

Table 2: On-Farm Nutrient Sources and Application Rates for Young Fruit Trees

Material NâPâK (approx.) Rate per Tree per Year Application Method Notes
Composted manure 1.5â0.5â1.5% 10â20 kg Ring at drip line, cover with mulch Age 3+ months; avoid fresh manure
Poultry litter (aged) 3â2â2% 5â10 kg Broadcast in ring, incorporate lightly High N; do not over-apply
Wood ash 0â1â5% 1â2 handfuls Sprinkle around drip line Raises pH; use sparingly
Legume mulch (e.g. Tephrosia) 2â0.2â1% 5â10 kg fresh Surface mulch around tree Also suppresses weeds

Sources: FAO, On-farm composting methods (Land and Water Discussion Paper 2, 2003); IFDC, Fertilizer Use and Crop Production in Africa (2020); KALRO soil fertility guidelines for smallholder orchards (2018).

5. Integrated Pest Management Using Local Plants and Traps

IPM means using the cheapest effective control firstâmonitoring, cultural practices, local botanicals, and trapsâand chemicals only as a last resort. This protects beneficial insects, reduces cost, and keeps fruit safe for market.

Local plant sprays: Neem leaves and seeds (soak 1 kg crushed seed in 10 L water for 24 hours, strain, spray) control aphids, whiteflies, and some caterpillars. Tephrosia and tobacco leaf extracts are also used. Chilli and garlic sprays deter chewing insects. Spray in the evening to avoid killing bees.

Traps: Yellow sticky traps catch whiteflies and aphids. Fruit fly traps made from plastic bottles with a sugar-yeast bait or a few drops of local brew reduce mango and citrus fly damage. Pheromone traps are available through extension services at low cost.

Cultural control: Remove and destroy fallen fruit to break pest cycles. Keep the orchard clean. Encourage natural enemies by planting flowering border plants such as sunflower and marigold. Rotate control methods so pests do not develop resistance.

6. Hands-On: Making a Simple Drip Irrigation System from Plastic Bottles

This is the lowest-cost irrigation method for young trees. You need one 1.5â2 L plastic bottle per tree, a nail or hot wire, and water.

  1. Clean the bottle and remove the label.
  2. Puncture 2â3 small holes in the cap using a nail or heated wire. The holes should be small enough that water drips slowly, not streams.
  3. Cut off the base of the bottle (or leave it intact and fill through the cap opening before sealing).
  4. Bury the bottle neck-down beside the tree, about 15â20 cm from the trunk, with the cap about 10 cm below the soil surface.
  5. Fill the bottle with water. It will drip into the root zone over 4â8 hours.
  6. Refill every 2â3 days in the dry season. Cover the top with a stone or lid to reduce evaporation and mosquito breeding.

For a 50-tree orchard, this system costs almost nothing and can keep young trees alive through a dry spell. It is not a substitute for a full irrigation system for mature trees, but it is the best entry-level option for smallholders.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Water young trees deeply every 3â7 days in the dry season; check soil moisture in the rainy season.
  • Maintain a 1 m weed-free ring around each tree; weed before seeds set.
  • Apply 7â10 cm of mulch, keeping a 10 cm gap around the trunk.
  • Train 3â5 scaffold branches in years 1â3; keep canopy below 3 m for easy harvest.
  • Apply aged manure or compost at the drip line at the start of the rains; never pile against the trunk.
  • Use neem, chilli, and garlic sprays plus yellow sticky and fruit fly traps before buying chemicals.
  • Install bottle drip irrigation for young trees before the dry season begins.
  • Wear gloves, closed shoes, and long trousers when pruning or clearing; keep a first-aid kit on site.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Irrigation Water Management: Irrigation Scheduling
  • FAO â On-farm Composting Methods
  • KALRO â Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (fruit tree and soil fertility manuals)
  • CABI â Integrated Pest Management Resources for Africa
  • IFAD â Smallholder Market Access and Rural Finance

Business note: Every technique in this module reduces cost or increases marketable yield. Track your cost per tree per seasonâwater, labour, mulch, compost, and pest control. Farmers who do this consistently find that the bottle drip system and on-farm compost pay for themselves within one season. Your orchard is not just a garden; it is a business. Manage it like one.

quiz.q: How much water does a 1-year-old fruit tree need in the dry season?
quiz.explanation: Young trees need about 10 liters every 2-3 days in dry conditions.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to water trees?
options: B) Early morning or late evening
quiz.explanation: Watering early or late reduces evaporation loss.

quiz.q: How can you tell if a young tree needs water?
options: B) Soil is dry 10 cm down
quiz.explanation: Check soil moisture 10 cm deep; if dry, water.

quiz.q: What should you do if leaves wilt in the morning?
quiz.explanation: Morning wilting means the tree is very dry and needs water right away.

quiz.q: In the rainy season, when should you stop watering?
options: B) If rain falls every week
quiz.explanation: If you get regular weekly rain, you can stop watering.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of mulching?
options: B) To conserve water and suppress weeds
C) To make the soil acidic
quiz.explanation: Mulch keeps soil moist and stops weeds from growing.

quiz.q: How thick should a mulch layer be around a tree?
quiz.explanation: A 5-10 cm layer is thick enough to conserve water and block weeds.

quiz.q: How far should mulch be kept from the tree trunk?
quiz.explanation: Keeping mulch 10 cm from the trunk prevents rot and pest damage.

quiz.q: What is a good living mulch for an orchard?
quiz.explanation: Legumes like beans cover the soil and add nitrogen.

quiz.q: How often should you weed during the rainy season?
quiz.explanation: Weeds grow fast in rains, so weed every 2 weeks.

quiz.q: Why should you remove water sprouts from the bottom of a young tree?
options: B) They steal energy from the tree
quiz.explanation: Water sprouts waste the tree's energy and should be removed.

quiz.q: What is the ideal number of main scaffold branches for a young fruit tree?
quiz.explanation: 3-5 well-spaced branches form a strong, open structure.

quiz.q: When is the best time to prune a young tree?
options: B) In the middle of the rainy season
quiz.explanation: Prune in the dry season when the tree is dormant to reduce stress.

quiz.q: What should you do with pruning cuts?
options: B) Cut at a slight angle above a bud
quiz.explanation: A clean angled cut above a bud helps the tree heal properly.

quiz.q: Why should you remove flowers in the first 3 years?
options: A) To make the tree taller
B) To let the tree grow roots and branches
quiz.explanation: Removing early flowers directs energy into strong vegetative growth.

quiz.q: What is the maximum height you should keep a fruit tree for easy harvest?
quiz.explanation: Keeping trees under 2.5 m means you can pick fruit without a ladder.

quiz.q: How long should fresh manure be left to rot before use?
quiz.explanation: Rotting for 2-3 months kills pathogens and prevents root burn.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to apply compost around a tree?
options: A) Dig it deep into the soil
B) Spread it in a ring 20 cm from the trunk
C) Pile it against the trunk
D) Mix it with water and spray leaves
quiz.explanation: Spread compost in a ring away from the trunk and cover with mulch.

quiz.q: How much compost should a mature tree get per year?
quiz.explanation: Mature trees need 4-6 buckets (40-60 liters) of compost annually.

quiz.q: What is manure tea?
options: B) Liquid fertilizer made by soaking manure in water
quiz.explanation: Manure tea is a quick liquid feed made by soaking manure in water.

quiz.q: Which material is 'green' for a compost pile?
quiz.explanation: Green materials are fresh and moist, like kitchen scraps and grass.

quiz.q: What does a good compost pile need?
options: B) Air, water, and a mix of green and brown materials
quiz.explanation: Compost needs air, moisture, and a balance of green and brown matter.

quiz.q: What is a simple trap for fruit flies?
options: A) A bottle with vinegar and sugar
quiz.explanation: Fruit flies are attracted to vinegar and sugar and drown in the bottle.

quiz.q: How do you make a neem spray?
options: A) Boil neem leaves for 1 minute
B) Soak crushed neem leaves in water for 24 hours
quiz.explanation: Soaking crushed neem leaves in water for 24 hours extracts the active compounds.

quiz.q: What is a good plant to repel nematodes?
quiz.explanation: Marigolds release compounds that repel nematodes in the soil.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid putting infested fruits in compost?
quiz.explanation: Infested fruits carry pests that can re-infest your orchard.

quiz.q: How many holes should you poke in a 2-liter bottle cap for drip irrigation?
quiz.explanation: 3-5 small holes give a slow drip that lasts 2-3 days.

quiz.q: Where should you bury the neck of the drip bottle?
options: B) 20 cm from the trunk, 10 cm deep
quiz.explanation: Bury the neck 20 cm from the trunk and 10 cm deep so water reaches roots.

quiz.q: How much water can a bottle drip system save compared to pouring from a bucket?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation saves up to 70% because water goes directly to roots.

quiz.q: What should you do if the drip holes get clogged?
options: B) Clean them with a needle
quiz.explanation: A needle clears the holes without making them too large.
